cards.name: Board space records and chain tables
cards.summary: A board loads as a flat array of space records that each carry a 3D position, a three-axis scale and a type byte, followed by two chain tables.
cards.behavior: A board file is read once into a temporary arena. The header supplies the space count and two chain counts. Each space position arrives packed as an integer triple and every component is multiplied by five world units as it lands in the record, so a board authored on a small integer grid occupies the scene at working scale without the file carrying large coordinates. The record keeps x, y and z apart, so a space can sit well above or below its neighbours and the graph is a 3D volume rather than a lane. Every space starts at unit scale on all three axes, and the highlight animations that later rewrite scale touch only x and z, so no pop or shrink can change the height an actor stands at. Two chain tables follow as variable-length runs of space indices; the second table is the one the position resolver and the length helper read, so a chain slot can be turned into an absolute space and therefore into world coordinates in two steps. Space types are bytes with ten defined values, and retyping a space is a single store on the record, which is how a plain space becomes a star space later in a match.

constants.name: space position scale
constants.unit: world units per source grid unit, applied once at load, no timestep

constants.name: space type count
constants.unit: count of defined space types, static, no timestep

constants.name: initial space scale
constants.unit: scale factor on each axis, static until an animation runs, no timestep

capabilities: load a board as a space graph with per-space height
resolve a chain slot to an absolute space index
retype a space at runtime

cards.name: Space cursor and lookahead
cards.summary: Each board actor keeps current and next chain plus current and next space, and seating it on a space seeds the lookahead one slot further along.
cards.behavior: Four indices describe where an actor stands: current chain, current space, next chain and next space. Seating an actor writes both current and next chain when a chain is supplied and, when a space is supplied, writes the current space and points the lookahead at the following slot of that chain. A second call rewrites only the lookahead fields a board wants to change, which is how a branch is taken: the lookahead chain is replaced and the lookahead space is reset to the head of the new chain while the actor's current space stays where it is. Keeping current and lookahead in separate fields is what lets an actor be visibly travelling toward a point while gameplay code still asks which space it occupies, and it means a walk can be retargeted by writing one pair of fields. Because the lookahead is a slot inside a chain rather than a position, the target coordinates are read from the space record at the moment the movement process starts, so the height of the destination comes from the graph and not from the actor.

constants.name: lookahead step
constants.unit: space slots along the chain, applied per seating, no timestep

capabilities: seed an actor's space cursor with a lookahead slot
retarget an actor onto another chain

cards.name: Space-to-space approach and turning
cards.summary: Actors cross a board with two interpolators: a fixed-distance step toward the next space and a counted turn onto the travel heading.
cards.behavior: Movement between spaces is a process the turn script waits on. The distance form takes the offset between the actor and the next space, derives its direction, multiplies by a fixed per-update travel and accumulates, stopping as soon as the remaining distance is under one travel step and then snapping exactly onto the destination, so an actor never idles between two spaces or drifts off the graph. The counted form divides the angle it must cover by the number of updates it was handed and applies that increment per update until the counter empties, which is how a turn in place is choreographed. Headings are absolute angles in degrees and the shortest arc is chosen by adding a full circle when the raw difference is negative and flipping the sign once the difference passes a half turn, so an actor never spins the long way round. Callers chain several of these, which is how a script turns an actor by a quarter circle, holds, continues, or hides the model, moves the anchor and then walks it the last stretch at the same fixed travel per update.

constants.name: approach travel
constants.unit: world units per update, rate unverified

constants.name: full circle
constants.unit: degrees, static wrap constant, no timestep

constants.name: half circle
constants.unit: degrees, static sign threshold, no timestep

capabilities: step an actor toward a target at a fixed travel per update
turn an actor by a counted arc
move an actor the last stretch after a reposition

cards.name: Board camera follow
cards.summary: A board process re-points the screen pan every update at either the active player's world position or a nominated space position.
cards.behavior: The follow loop sets the pan divisor and the travel cap once at start-up and then runs for the life of the scene. On each update it takes either the current player's 3D position or a designated space's 3D position, converts that point to screen space and hands it to the pan routine. Smoothing is not done here: the pan routine divides the remaining offset by the divisor and limits the per-update travel to the cap, so the same follow process can be made snappy or lazy per scene. Because the input is a world position rather than a screen position, an actor that hops or stands on a raised space drags the view with it in height as well as across the board, and re-targeting costs nothing more than the current player index changing. A negative cap disables the clamp, which the board uses while it is still framing the scene at start-up.

constants.name: pan divisor
constants.unit: divisor applied to the pan offset each update, rate unverified

constants.name: pan travel cap
constants.unit: scaled screen units of pan travel per update, rate unverified

capabilities: follow a moving 3D point with a screen pan
retarget the follow to a fixed board space

cards.name: Turn rotation and actor re-seating
cards.summary: Rotating the turn increments the active player with a wrap at four slots, then re-seats every actor from its space record.
cards.behavior: The rotate entry point increments the active player index and wraps to the first slot once it reaches the roster size. It then loops over all four player records and does the same work for each: refresh per-player visual state, clear the hidden flag on the actor, recompute the actor's position from its current chain and space, and reset the facing offset used to keep co-located actors apart. Re-seating everybody rather than only the new active player is what repairs actors that an event displaced, left mid-animation, or left standing on a space whose type changed during the previous turn. Because the position is recomputed from the space record instead of being remembered, an actor that walked off a raised platform returns at the correct height instead of at some average plane, and the world position of every actor is guaranteed to agree with the graph at the moment a turn begins.

constants.name: roster size
constants.unit: players, static, no timestep

capabilities: advance the active player with a wrap
snap every board actor back onto its space position

cards.name: Landed space coin effect
cards.summary: Resolving a landed space maps its type to a turn status and handles the two plain coin spaces inline with a short settle pause.
cards.behavior: The resolve step reads the active actor's current chain and space, fetches the space record and converts the space type into a compact turn status that other systems read. It runs on the slot the actor actually reached in the graph, so the effect follows the 3D position the move ended at rather than an assumed one, and a space that changed type mid-turn already resolves as its new type. Two types are special-cased. One awards three coins and the other removes three; both spawn the floating coin indicator, run the coin tally animation, play a distinct sound and wait thirty updates before returning, so the change is legible before the next beat of the turn. Every other space type falls through to the event list the board attached to that space at load time, which is why only these two plain coin spaces live in this path. Award and forfeit differ only in sign, so the ledger sees one code path and the clamp at zero is inherited rather than re-implemented for the negative case.

constants.name: awarded coins
constants.unit: coins, applied once per landing, no timestep

constants.name: forfeited coins
constants.unit: coins, applied once per landing, no timestep

constants.name: settle pause
constants.unit: updates, rate unverified

capabilities: apply a signed coin delta when a move resolves
hold the turn while a coin change reads on screen

cards.name: Junction prompt and branch
cards.summary: At a branch the board builds a prompt from a shared choice table, resolves a human or canned CPU answer, then rewrites the lookahead chain.
cards.behavior: The branch is staged rather than instantaneous. The script waits for the actor's walk to finish, stops the walk animation, then builds a prompt object from a shared table of choices and attaches it to the active player. A human answers by steering and confirming. A CPU answers differently: the board reads a per-board counter, indexes a table of stored answers with it, feeds that stored code into the prompt object that many times and then feeds a second code once, before the prompt resolves through exactly the same call a human answer goes through, which is what keeps a CPU branch and a player branch from diverging. When the prompt reports a positive answer the board rewrites the lookahead chain with a different chain index and resets the lookahead space to the head of that chain. The actor's current space is untouched, so the branch is followed by an ordinary space-to-space walk to a new 3D destination, with the destination's height read from the graph rather than assumed.

constants.name: canned answer code, repeated
constants.unit: prompt answer code, one per stored answer, no timestep

constants.name: canned answer code, final
constants.unit: prompt answer code, once per branch, no timestep

constants.name: branch chain index
constants.unit: chain index, one per branch, no timestep

capabilities: offer a branch choice at a junction
auto-answer a branch for a CPU actor
retarget the lookahead onto another chain

cards.name: Camera slots and default projection
cards.summary: Six camera slots are allocated with a 45 degree vertical view, 80 and 8000 clip planes, a four-thirds aspect and a game-level orbit rig pitched back and zoomed out.
cards.behavior: Bring-up allocates six slot structures and fills every one with the same projection: a 45 degree vertical field of view, a near plane at 80 world units and a far plane at 8000, plus a viewport rectangle and a scissor rectangle that scenes overwrite later. The projection is rebuilt on request from the slot's stored angle and clip values with the aspect fixed at four thirds, taking the eye, look-at and up vectors from the slot, so a scene never edits a matrix directly. The orbit rig used by cinematic and arena scenes is separate from the slots: it starts with its rotation x component at 325 degrees, which frames the same as a 35 degree downward tilt, y and z at zero, a zoom scalar of 2250 world units and its centre on the origin. Scenes then animate only those orbit values, which is why one set of defaults can serve a distant board overview and a close arena without reallocating a slot.

cards.name: Distance-banded clip planes
cards.summary: The pan process widens the clip range in three distance bands and eases a screen offset toward the projected look-at point.
cards.behavior: Each update the pan process measures how far the look-at point is from the eye and rewrites that slot's near and far planes accordingly. Under five thousand units it keeps 80 and 8000, under fifteen thousand it opens to 1000 and 20000, and beyond that it opens to 3000 and 28000. The vertical field of view is left alone, so the framing never changes, only the depth range: close-in play keeps fine depth resolution and a zoomed-out overview stops clipping the far side of a tall board. The same process then builds the screen-space correction between the projected target and the current offset, snaps when the correction falls under one of its scaled units, and otherwise normalises it, limits it by the travel cap and accumulates it. Scaling by four around that comparison is what gives the pan sub-pixel resolution while the visible motion stays on whole pixels.

cards.name: Minigame camera bring-up
cards.summary: A minigame overlay brings up one camera, zeroes the orbit rig, sets a long zoom and views the arena through a ten degree lens.
cards.behavior: Bring-up allocates a single camera slot for the overlay, then resets the orbit rig to a neutral pose: rotation zero on all three axes, the centre at the origin and the zoom scalar pushed out to 2000 world units. It then overwrites the slot's projection with a ten degree vertical field of view and the usual 80 and 8000 clip planes, so the arena is seen through a long narrow lens instead of the board's 45 degree one. A narrow lens at a long zoom compresses depth, which keeps a wide flat arena legible and stops distant scenery from dominating the frame, and the near plane stays far enough out that floor geometry beneath the camera cannot intrude. Everything an overlay does afterwards is animation of the orbit rotation, the centre and the zoom, so the projection is built once and never rebuilt mid-match.

constants.unit: world units, static at bring-up, no timestep

cards.name: Scripted zoom dolly
cards.summary: A three-stage script holds a wide framing for about forty-six updates, ramps the zoom and the centre for thirty, then locks a closer framing.
cards.behavior: The script is a small state machine driven by an object callback. In the first stage it rewrites the same framing every update, a zoom of 2766 world units with the orbit rotation x held at 309 degrees and the centre offset above the arena floor, which pins the camera still for about forty-six updates while the scene settles. In the second stage, held for thirty updates, the zoom grows by a fixed increment and the centre x grows by two per update while the rotation is left alone, so the camera dollies in and tracks sideways without pitching. The numbers are exact: thirty steps of the zoom increment add the 1100 units that separate 2766 from 3866, and thirty steps of two units on the centre x add the 60 units that separate the stage-one centre from the stage-three centre, so the final stage can simply write the end values with no visible seam. The third stage writes those end values once and clears the callback.

constants.name: hold updates
constants.unit: updates, rate unverified

constants.name: start zoom
constants.unit: world units, static during stage one, no timestep

constants.name: ramp updates
constants.unit: updates, rate unverified

constants.name: zoom step
constants.unit: world units per update, rate unverified

constants.name: centre step
constants.unit: world units per update on the x axis, rate unverified

constants.name: end zoom
constants.unit: world units, static during stage three, no timestep

cards.name: Match length by play type
cards.summary: Match length comes from a three-entry play-type table, with a shorter table when a modifier flag is set, and turn numbering starts at one.
cards.behavior: When a match initialises with a save flag clear, the play type selects one of three lengths: twenty, thirty-five or fifty turns. If a second modifier flag is set the same three play types map to ten, twenty or thirty instead, which offers a shorter session without a second play-type list. The current turn starts at one and the active player index resets to the first slot, so turns elapsed can be derived as the maximum minus the current plus one and the progress readout and the CPU turn-progress guard share that one derivation instead of each counting turns themselves. The same initialisation clears per-player counters, stars and coin totals, so a new match never inherits statistics from the previous one. The turn limit is also the budget for board traversal: every turn is one walk through the 3D space graph for one actor, so the length chosen here sets how many times the board is crossed before scoring.

cards.name: CPU decision walk and weighted answer
cards.summary: The CPU walks a typed node table, stops at the first passing guard, and resolves a packed weighted binary choice through a percentage roll.
cards.behavior: A decision is a flat array of nodes with a type in the high byte and two data words. Guards ask, in order, whether the acting player holds at least a given number of coins, whether a mask of board flags is satisfied, whether a bit named by a global index is set, how a shared board counter compares with a constant under one of six relations, whether a bit named by a per-player query is set, whether a callback returns non-zero, and whether enough turns have elapsed. The walk falls through a failing guard to the next node and stops at the first that passes. The chosen leaf's second word is either a negative value read as a jump or a packed answer: two weights and a one-bit outcome, where the low byte supplies the weight at the lowest difficulty step and the high byte supplies it otherwise, and the outcome bit selects which way the answer falls. The answer is what a board consumes to pick a lookahead chain and therefore which 3D destination the actor walks toward, so the whole tree is the decision layer above the space graph's traversal. The percentage helper maps one byte of the engine stream onto the range nought to ninety-nine, so a weight is literally the chance of taking the intended branch: packing thirty and seventy produces a cautious actor, and swapping them produces an aggressive one with no new decision code.

constants.unit: flags checked in one mask, static, no timestep

constants.name: low weight mask
constants.unit: bit mask, static, no timestep

constants.name: high weight shift
constants.unit: bits, static, no timestep

constants.name: outcome bit
constants.unit: bit value, static, no timestep

constants.name: percent span
constants.unit: percent, evaluated per roll, no timestep

cards.name: Engine random stream
cards.summary: One 32-bit state feeds every random draw through a multiplier-plus-increment step and returns the second byte of the new state.
cards.behavior: The engine keeps a single 32-bit seed. Each draw advances it by multiplying the seed by a large odd constant and adding a fixed increment, wrapping at 32 bits, and returns bits sixteen through twenty-three of the new state. The stream is therefore fully deterministic from whatever the seed held at boot, which is what makes a recorded input sequence replayable and a CPU test repeatable. Because there is exactly one global stream, board junctions, the selection of which space in the 3D graph is marked as the live star, star prices and every minigame arena layout draw from the same sequence, so any change in how many draws one system consumes shifts every later draw in the session. Mechanics that must not repeat a value (a reroll equal to the previous roll, a pick equal to the previous pick) loop on the generator and spend one extra draw per rejection rather than reseeding, which keeps the disturbance to the rest of the session bounded and predictable.

constants.name: multiplier
constants.unit: scalar, applied once per draw with 32-bit wrap, no timestep

constants.name: increment
constants.unit: scalar, applied once per draw with 32-bit wrap, no timestep

constants.name: output shift
constants.unit: bits, static, no timestep

capabilities: generate deterministic pseudo-random bytes

cards.name: Star space rotation
cards.summary: A board keeps seven candidate star spaces with priority values, advances which candidate is live and rewrites the space types that show it.
cards.behavior: The candidates live in two parallel lists, a space index per candidate and a priority per candidate, and the shuffle permutes both columns together. The shuffle runs a fixed number of passes; each pass draws two candidate slots, skips the pass when the slots match or when the priority comparison fails, and otherwise swaps both columns. Comparing against the priority column rather than shuffling uniformly is what biases the permutation so higher priority candidates migrate toward the front. Advancing the live index then wraps when it runs past the last candidate, sets a board flag marking that the rotation has cycled, reshuffles, and swaps the head and tail when the wrap would otherwise hand out the same space twice in a row. Marking writes the live candidate with one space type and every already visited candidate with another, so the board shows a single live star plus a trail of used ones without a second data structure, and because the type lives on the space record the mark inherits that space's position and height for free.

constants.name: shuffle passes
constants.unit: passes, run once per rotation, no timestep

constants.name: candidate slots
constants.unit: candidate indices, static, no timestep

constants.name: visited space type
constants.unit: space type code, static, no timestep

constants.name: live star space type
constants.unit: space type code, static, no timestep

capabilities: shuffle candidate star spaces with a priority bias

cards.name: Coin-gated star purchase
cards.summary: A star costs twenty coins, is refused at a cap of ninety-nine stars, and a confirmed purchase debits immediately and then plays a lift-and-arc award.
cards.behavior: The gate runs before any prompt appears. A player already at the star cap is refused outright, then a coin total under twenty produces the shortfall text, and only a player past both tests sees the confirmation prompt. The prompt's answer is handled three ways: one answer relaunches the visit instead of deciding, one shows an explanatory message and charges nothing, and the remaining answer applies a single signed debit equal to the price, written as a signed hex literal, and then starts the award sequence. The award lifts a star prop two hundred world units above the anchor where the sale happened, then carries it toward a second anchor while adding a sine arc a hundred units tall and spinning it about the vertical axis, so the sale reads as an object rising and travelling rather than a counter changing. The player's star count is incremented by that award sequence and not by the gate, so an interrupted or declined purchase never grants a star.

constants.unit: stars, checked once per visit, no timestep

constants.name: price gate
constants.unit: coins, checked once per visit, no timestep

constants.unit: coins, applied once per purchase, no timestep

constants.name: award lift

constants.unit: world units, one-off per animation step, rate unverified
